questions.question: A dairy farm in the hills of New York lies far nearer to Lake Ontario than to the Chesapeake Bay. The creeks on its land run south into a river, and the river empties into the bay. Which watershed is the farm in?
questions.answer: The bay's, as its creeks drain there
choices: The bay's, as its creeks drain there
The lake's, as the lake lies much nearer
Both, as it lies between the two
Neither, as it is far from both
questions.context: A watershed is all the land that drains to one outlet, so the farm lies in the bay's watershed however far away it is: rain on its fields, and whatever the rain washes off them, can travel down its creeks and the river to the bay. Being near a lake does not put land in the lake's watershed; only where its water drains does. The bay's watershed spreads over about 166,000 square kilometres in six states and the District of Columbia.
questions.grade_note: Texas's grade-7 standard 7.11A has students analyse human influences on the water of a watershed, the land that drains to one river, lake or bay.

questions.question: Scientists mapping the watershed of a river in hilly country trace its edge on the ground by walking the whole way round it. Along most of the walk, what kind of ground are they on?
questions.answer: The tops of ridges and hills
choices: The tops of ridges and hills
The banks of the river's creeks
The edges of marshes and ponds
The floors of the valleys
questions.context: A watershed's edge is its divide, the high ground where the rain parts: rain on one side drains to this river, and rain on the other side to the next. The river and its creeks run through the low middle of the watershed, not along its edge. North America's Continental Divide follows the Rocky Mountains and sends water on one side toward the Pacific and on the other toward the Atlantic.
questions.grade_note: Texas 7.11A treats a watershed as a system of landforms, surface water and groundwater; the divides are the landforms that bound it.

questions.question: Under a farm lie four layers of rock and sediment, all below the water table, where every space in the ground is full of water. One layer, the clay, holds the most water of the four, since more than half of it is space between its tiny grains. Which layer should a well draw from to give the most water?
choices: The gravel
The clay
The silt
The granite
questions.context: Gravel has less empty space than clay, but its spaces are large and joined, so water flows through it easily and a well in it refills fast: gravel is permeable as well as porous. Clay's spaces are so tiny and poorly linked that water barely moves through it, and silt, with grains between the two in size, lets water through only slowly. Solid granite has almost no spaces at all and gives water only where it is cracked.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade earth science teaches porosity and permeability, and that a good aquifer must be both porous and permeable.

questions.question: A family's shallow well has given good water for years. Then a bottling company drills a big well into the same ground a short walk away and pumps it day and night. Within weeks the family's well runs dry, though rain has fallen as usual. What has happened?
questions.answer: The company's pumping lowered the water table
choices: The company's pumping lowered the water table
The company's drilling cut off an underground stream
The company's pumping emptied the whole aquifer
The company's drilling shook loose mud into the well
questions.context: Pumping lowers the water table around a well in a dip shaped like a funnel, called a cone of depression, deepest at the pump. When the cone reaches a shallow well nearby, the water table there sinks below the well's bottom and the well goes dry, though the ground deeper down is still soaked. Groundwater fills the spaces in soil and rock rather than flowing in underground streams, and the usual fix is to drill the shallow well deeper.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches the water table, and that a well runs dry when pumping or drought lowers the water table below its bottom.

questions.question: A town spreads over its fields and woods, covering much of the ground with roads, roofs and parking lots. After heavy storms its creek now floods higher than it used to. What has the paving done to the groundwater beneath the town?
questions.answer: Less rain soaks down to refill it
choices: Less rain soaks down to refill it
More rain soaks down to refill it
Its weight squeezes the water out
Nothing, as the water lies so deep
questions.context: Rain cannot soak through pavement, so it runs off into drains and the creek instead of seeping down to refill the groundwater, and the water table can sink. In the most built-up places 70 to 90 percent of the rain can run off, against 10 to 20 percent in wild country. That same groundwater feeds creeks between storms, so paved towns often see creeks that flood higher after rain and run lower in dry spells.
questions.grade_note: Texas's grade-7 standard teaches that the more of an area is paved over, the less of its rain becomes groundwater.

questions.question: A big dam is built across a river, and a long lake fills up behind it. In the decades that follow, the beaches and the delta where the river meets the sea begin to wear away. What has the dam done with the sand and mud that once built them?
questions.answer: Trapped most of it on the lake bed
choices: Trapped most of it on the lake bed
Swept it out past the beaches into deep water
Ground it to dust in its turbines
Spread it over the fields along the river
questions.context: The lake's still water slows the river, so the sand and mud it carries settle to the bottom: big reservoirs trap most of what flows in, and Lake Nasser behind Egypt's Aswan High Dam holds back over 95 percent of the Nile's. With little sand coming down to replace what the waves carry off, the coast wears back, and the Nile delta's shore has retreated faster since the dam was finished in 1970. The dam also stops the floods that once spread fresh silt over the fields along the river.
questions.grade_note: NGSS MS-ESS3-3 and Texas 7.11A have seventh graders study how dams change a river and the land and coast downstream.

questions.question: Each summer a dead zone forms where a great river meets the sea: near the sea floor, the water holds so little oxygen that most fish leave or die. Fertiliser washed off farms across the river's huge watershed feeds it. One spring, weeks of heavy rain soak those farms. How will that summer's dead zone most likely compare with those of other years?
questions.answer: Larger, as more fertiliser washes down to the sea
choices: Larger, as more fertiliser washes down to the sea
Smaller, as the extra water thins out the fertiliser
Smaller, as the rainwater brings more oxygen with it
About the same, as the rain falls so far from the sea
questions.context: Rain washes fertiliser off fields all over the watershed, and the swollen river carries more of it to the sea, so the algae it feeds grow thicker; when they die and sink, the bacteria that rot them use up more of the deep water's oxygen. Fresh river water floats on the salty sea, so little new oxygen mixes down to the bottom. Wet springs, as in 2019, bring large dead zones, and the drought of 2012 brought one of the smallest on record.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards (Texas 7.11A and 7.11B) teach how human activity across a watershed harms its rivers and the sea they reach.

questions.question: Farmers in California's San Joaquin Valley pumped groundwater from its deep layers of sand and clay for decades to water their crops. By the 1970s the ground had sunk by more than 8 metres in places. Why did the ground sink?
questions.answer: Its clay packed tighter as the water was pumped out
choices: Its clay packed tighter as the water was pumped out
Caves left by drained underground lakes fell in
The weight of crops and farm machines pressed it down
Earthquakes along a fault dropped the valley floor
questions.context: The water in the spaces between grains helps carry the weight of the ground above. As pumping drew the water out, that weight pressed the clay's grains closer together, the clay layers thinned, and the land sank, mostly for good, so the squeezed clay can never again hold as much water. Collapsing caves make sinkholes in limestone country, but sand and clay hold no caves, and groundwater does not lie in underground lakes.
questions.grade_note: CK-12's middle-school earth science teaches that pumping an aquifer faster than it is recharged can make the ground above it sink.

questions.question: Two fish populations each lose the same share of their numbers to fishing boats every year. Sardines are usually ready to breed by the end of their first year. The orange roughy, a fish of the deep sea, does not breed until it is at least 20 years old, though it may live for more than a century. Which population will most likely shrink faster?
questions.answer: The orange roughy's, as it breeds so late
choices: The orange roughy's, as it breeds so late
The sardines', as more of them are caught
The sardines', as each lives only a few years
Both alike, as each loses the same share
questions.context: A population is overfished when fishing takes its fish faster than breeding replaces them. Sardines are ready to breed within about a year and spawn many times a season, so young fish soon fill the gaps, but an orange roughy caught at 15 never bred at all, and its young take decades to replace the old. Many orange roughy stocks were badly depleted within 3 to 20 years of fishing, and about a third of the sea fish stocks that scientists track are overfished.
questions.grade_note: Texas 7.11B has seventh graders explain how human activities such as fishing change ocean systems.

questions.question: Bottles, bags and lost fishing nets drift out to sea from coasts all around the Pacific. Some of this rubbish collects in one vast stretch of the North Pacific, far from any land, roughly midway between Hawaii and California. What gathers it there?
questions.answer: Currents that slowly circle the ocean
choices: Currents that slowly circle the ocean
Tides that pull it away from the coasts
Ships that dump their rubbish in that spot
Waves that roll it out from the beaches
questions.context: Winds and Earth's spin keep the surface water of each great ocean turning in a vast loop called a gyre, and floating rubbish drifts toward the calm middle of the loop and stays there. The garbage patch is no floating island: most of its pieces, by count, are bits of plastic smaller than 5 millimetres, so scattered that a boat can sail through and see little. Tides only carry water in and out along the coasts, and waves push floating things toward the shore, not away from it.
questions.grade_note: Texas 7.11B asks seventh graders to explain how human activities affect the ocean; plastic gathered by the gyres is one such effect.
